notice: RN bank batch 9: Respiratory II: chest tubes, ventilators, airway care and ARDS. Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md.

questions.stem: The nurse notices continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber of a client's chest drainage system. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the finding as expected
Check the system for an air leak, starting at the client's chest
Clamp the chest tube near the client
Increase the suction

rationale.correct: Intermittent bubbling in the water seal can be expected with a pneumothorax as air leaves the chest, but continuous bubbling means an air leak.

perOption.a: Continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber isn't expected.
perOption.b: Continuous bubbling means air is entering the system; the nurse checks the dressing and connections to find the leak.
perOption.c: Clamping can cause a tension pneumothorax and is done only briefly to locate a leak, per policy.
perOption.d: More suction doesn't fix a leak.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to an air leak in a chest drainage system.

questions.stem: A client's chest tube separates from the drainage system tubing. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Clamp the chest tube with a hemostat for 1 hour
Put the end of the chest tube 2 to 4 cm (1 to 2 inches) into a bottle of sterile water
Remove the chest tube
Cover the end of the tube with gauze

rationale.correct: If the chest tube disconnects, create a water seal right away, then reconnect a new sterile system.

perOption.a: Prolonged clamping risks a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.b: This creates a temporary water seal that keeps air from entering the chest.
perOption.c: The tube shouldn't be removed.
perOption.d: Gauze doesn't create a seal.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage a disconnected chest tube.

questions.stem: A client's chest tube is accidentally pulled out. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reinsert the chest tube
Cover the site with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides
Leave the site open to air
Apply a fully sealed dressing and watch the client

rationale.correct: Cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides, assess for respiratory distress and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Only a provider inserts a chest tube.
perOption.b: A dressing taped on three sides lets air escape but stops air from entering.
perOption.c: An open site lets air into the pleural space.
perOption.d: A fully sealed dressing can trap air and cause a tension pneumothorax.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond when a chest tube comes out.

questions.stem: Which actions are appropriate when caring for a client with a chest tube connected to wet suction? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the drainage system below the level of the chest
Keep the tubing free of dependent loops
Expect fluctuation (tidaling) in the water seal chamber with breathing
Expect gentle, continuous bubbling in the suction control chamber
Clamp the tube whenever the client is moved
Strip or milk the tubing routinely every hour

rationale.correct: Chest tube care: keep the system below the chest, avoid loops, expect tidaling and gentle suction bubbling, and don't clamp or strip routinely.

perOption.a: Gravity prevents backflow into the pleural space.
perOption.b: Loops collect fluid and impede drainage.
perOption.c: Tidaling shows the system is working and the lung isn't fully expanded.
perOption.d: Gentle bubbling means the suction is working.
perOption.e: Routine clamping risks a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.f: Routine stripping creates high negative pressure and is done only if ordered.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Care for a client with a chest tube.

questions.stem: For each chamber of the client's chest drainage system, select the finding that requires follow-up.

options.text: 150 mL of bright red drainage in the last hour
40 mL of serosanguineous drainage over 8 hours
Water level rises and falls with breathing
Constant bubbling
Gentle, continuous bubbling
No bubbling with the wall suction turned on

rationale.correct: Know what is expected in each chamber of the chest drainage system.

perOption.a: More than about 100 mL/hr of bright red drainage suggests hemorrhage.
perOption.b: This is expected drainage.
perOption.c: Tidaling is expected.
perOption.d: Continuous bubbling indicates an air leak.
perOption.e: This shows the suction is working.
perOption.f: No bubbling means the suction isn't working, for example because of a loose connection or a low setting.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess a chest drainage system.

questions.stem: After a car crash, a client has severe shortness of breath, absent breath sounds on the left and a trachea that has shifted to the right. The blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg and the neck veins are distended. What does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Left tension pneumothorax
Right simple pneumothorax
Pulmonary contusion
Flail chest

rationale.correct: Tension pneumothorax is an emergency treated with needle decompression and then a chest tube.

perOption.a: Air trapped in the left chest shifts the trachea and mediastinum away from that side and lowers cardiac output.
perOption.b: The trachea shifts away from a tension pneumothorax; here the problem is on the left.
perOption.c: A contusion doesn't shift the trachea.
perOption.d: Flail chest causes paradoxical chest wall movement.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A client has several fractured ribs after a fall. Which finding suggests a flail chest?

options.text: Part of the chest wall moves in during inhalation and out during exhalation
Barrel chest
Crackling under the skin when touched
Dullness to percussion

rationale.correct: Flail chest occurs when several adjacent ribs break in more than one place; the segment moves opposite to the rest of the chest.

perOption.a: Paradoxical movement of the chest wall segment is the sign of flail chest.
perOption.b: This is associated with COPD.
perOption.c: This is subcutaneous emphysema.
perOption.d: This suggests fluid or blood in the chest.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize flail chest.

questions.stem: The high-pressure alarm sounds on a client's ventilator. The client is coughing, and the nurse hears coarse rhonchi. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Suction the client's airway
Silence the alarm and recheck in 15 minutes
Check for a disconnection in the circuit
Increase the tidal volume

rationale.correct: High-pressure alarms come from obstruction (secretions, kinks, biting, coughing, bronchospasm); low-pressure alarms come from leaks or disconnections.

perOption.a: Secretions raise airway pressure; suctioning clears them.
perOption.b: Alarms must be investigated, not just silenced.
perOption.c: Disconnections cause low-pressure alarms.
perOption.d: This would raise the pressure further.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a high-pressure ventilator alarm.

questions.stem: The low-pressure alarm sounds on a client's ventilator. What should the nurse check first?

options.text: The ventilator tubing connections
The client's airway for secretions
Whether the client is biting the tube
The client's sedation level

rationale.correct: Low pressure means air is escaping: check the connections, the circuit and the cuff.

perOption.a: A disconnection or leak is the most common cause of a low-pressure alarm.
perOption.b: Secretions cause high-pressure alarms.
perOption.c: Biting causes high-pressure alarms.
perOption.d: This isn't the first check for low pressure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a low-pressure ventilator alarm.

questions.stem: A client's ventilator alarm sounds, the client's SpO2 is falling and the nurse can't find the cause. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Silence the alarm and call the respiratory therapist
Disconnect the client from the ventilator and ventilate manually with a bag-valve device, then call for help
Increase the oxygen on the ventilator to 100% and wait
Reintubate the client

rationale.correct: If the cause of an alarm can't be found quickly and the client is in distress, ventilate manually with a bag-valve device.

perOption.a: The client needs ventilation now.
perOption.b: Manual ventilation supports the client while the problem is found.
perOption.c: This may not help if the problem is mechanical.
perOption.d: Only qualified providers reintubate, and the tube may be in place.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support a ventilated client when the cause of an alarm is unknown.

questions.stem: Which actions help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 to 45 degrees
Interrupt sedation daily and assess readiness to wean, as prescribed
Provide regular oral care
Drain condensation in the tubing away from the client
Keep the client flat to prevent pressure injuries
Change the ventilator circuit every day

rationale.correct: The VAP bundle includes head-of-bed elevation, daily sedation breaks, oral care and careful circuit management.

perOption.a: Elevation reduces aspiration of gastric contents.
perOption.b: Daily sedation breaks shorten ventilation time.
perOption.c: Oral care reduces bacteria that can be aspirated.
perOption.d: Draining toward the client can wash bacteria into the airway.
perOption.f: Circuits are changed only when soiled or malfunctioning.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: Right after a client is intubated, the nurse hears breath sounds on the right side but none on the left. What does this suggest?

options.text: The tube is correctly placed
The tube is in the right mainstem bronchus
The tube is in the esophagus
The client has a left pneumothorax

rationale.correct: Confirm tube placement with end-tidal CO2, equal breath sounds and a chest x-ray.

perOption.a: Breath sounds should be equal on both sides.
perOption.b: The right bronchus is straighter, so a tube inserted too far tends to enter it; it needs to be pulled back.
perOption.c: An esophageal tube causes absent breath sounds on both sides and sounds over the stomach.
perOption.d: This is possible but less likely right after intubation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize right mainstem intubation.

questions.stem: The nurse is suctioning a client's tracheostomy. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Perform hand hygiene and put on PPE
Apply intermittent suction while rotating and withdrawing the catheter, for no more than 10 to 15 seconds
Re-oxygenate the client before another pass
Insert the catheter without applying suction

rationale.correct: Use sterile technique, pre-oxygenate, insert without suction, suction while withdrawing for 15 seconds or less, then re-oxygenate.

perOption.a: Infection control comes first.
perOption.b: Pre-oxygenating reduces hypoxemia during suctioning.
perOption.c: Suction during insertion damages the mucosa and removes oxygen.
perOption.d: Limiting the time prevents hypoxemia.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Suction a tracheostomy safely.

questions.stem: Which items should be kept at the bedside of a client with a new tracheostomy?

options.text: A spare tracheostomy tube of the same size and one size smaller, with the obturator
A tongue blade and a penlight
A nasal cannula only
A urinary catheter kit

rationale.correct: Keep an obturator, a spare tube (same size and one smaller), suction equipment and a bag-valve device at the bedside.

perOption.a: These allow quick replacement if the tube comes out.
perOption.b: These aren't essential for airway emergencies.
perOption.c: This isn't enough for an airway emergency.
perOption.d: This isn't related to airway safety.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare emergency equipment for a client with a tracheostomy.

questions.stem: What is the recommended pressure range for a tracheostomy or endotracheal tube cuff?

options.text: 5 to 10 cm H2O
20 to 30 cm H2O
40 to 50 cm H2O
60 to 70 cm H2O

rationale.correct: Cuff pressure of 20 to 30 cm H2O prevents aspiration and tracheal injury.

perOption.a: This is too low to seal the airway and prevent aspiration.
perOption.b: This seals the airway without cutting off blood flow to the tracheal mucosa.
perOption.c: This high pressure can cause tracheal ischemia and necrosis.
perOption.d: This would cause tracheal injury.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Maintain safe cuff pressure.

questions.stem: A client with sepsis is receiving 80% oxygen by face mask. The PaO2 is 55 mm Hg, and the chest x-ray shows bilateral infiltrates without heart failure. What does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
COPD exacerbation
Asthma attack
Atelectasis

rationale.correct: ARDS shows hypoxemia that doesn't improve with oxygen and bilateral infiltrates without a cardiac cause.

perOption.a: Refractory hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates after an insult such as sepsis suggests ARDS.
perOption.b: COPD doesn't cause new bilateral infiltrates with refractory hypoxemia.
perOption.c: Asthma doesn't cause bilateral infiltrates.
perOption.d: Atelectasis usually responds to oxygen and deep breathing.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize ARDS.

questions.stem: A client with ARDS is placed in the prone position. What is the purpose of this intervention?

options.text: To prevent pressure injuries
To improve oxygenation by better matching ventilation and blood flow
To make suctioning easier
To reduce sedation needs

rationale.correct: Prone positioning recruits collapsed alveoli and improves oxygenation in moderate to severe ARDS.

perOption.a: Prone positioning increases the risk of pressure injuries on the face and chest.
perOption.b: Prone positioning opens collapsed back regions of the lungs and improves oxygenation.
perOption.c: This isn't the main purpose.
perOption.d: This isn't the purpose.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain why prone positioning is used in ARDS.

questions.stem: In a restaurant, an adult is clutching the throat, can't speak and is making high-pitched sounds. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage the person to keep coughing
Give abdominal thrusts
Begin chest compressions
Perform a blind finger sweep

rationale.correct: Severe airway obstruction in a conscious adult: abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive.

perOption.a: Inability to speak means the obstruction is severe; coughing isn't enough.
perOption.b: Abdominal thrusts are used for a conscious adult with a severe airway obstruction.
perOption.c: Compressions start only if the person becomes unresponsive.
perOption.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Relieve a severe airway obstruction in a conscious adult.

questions.stem: An adult choking victim becomes unresponsive. After calling for help, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep giving abdominal thrusts with the victim standing
Begin CPR, looking in the mouth for the object before each set of breaths
Do a blind finger sweep
Wait for the emergency team before doing anything

rationale.correct: For an unresponsive choking victim, start CPR and check the mouth before giving breaths.

perOption.a: The victim must be lowered to the ground.
perOption.b: Chest compressions can dislodge the object; remove it only if it can be seen.
perOption.c: Blind sweeps aren't recommended.
perOption.d: Delaying CPR worsens outcomes.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond when a choking victim becomes unresponsive.

questions.stem: A client has had a left pneumonectomy for lung cancer. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: On the right (non-operative) side
On the back or turned partly toward the operative side
Prone
Flat in the Trendelenburg position

rationale.correct: After pneumonectomy, avoid complete lateral positioning on either side; position on the back or partly on the operative side, per the surgeon's orders.

perOption.a: Lying on the remaining lung can shift the mediastinum and compress that lung.
perOption.b: This lets the remaining lung expand fully and avoids shifting the mediastinum.
perOption.c: Prone positioning isn't used after pneumonectomy.
perOption.d: This reduces lung expansion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Position a client after pneumonectomy.

questions.stem: Which client meets the criteria for annual low-dose CT screening for lung cancer?

options.text: A 45-year-old who has never smoked
A 62-year-old with a 30 pack-year history who quit 5 years ago
A 72-year-old who quit smoking 25 years ago
A 40-year-old who smokes 1 pack a day

rationale.correct: USPSTF: annual low-dose CT for adults 50 to 80 with a history of 20 or more pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.

perOption.a: This client is too young and has no smoking history.
perOption.b: Screening is recommended for adults 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years.
perOption.c: Quitting more than 15 years ago puts this client outside the criteria.
perOption.d: This client is too young.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify clients who meet lung cancer screening criteria.

questions.stem: A client has smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes a day for 30 years. How many pack-years is this?

rationale.correct: Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked = 1.5 × 30 = 45 pack-years.
references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a smoking history in pack-years.

questions.stem: A client with obstructive sleep apnea has been prescribed CPAP. Which statement shows understanding?

options.text: "I'll use it only on nights when I feel very tired."
"I'll wear it every time I sleep, including naps."
"I'll take a sleeping pill to help me get used to it."
"I'll stop using it if the mask leaks."

rationale.correct: CPAP works only when used for all sleep; avoid alcohol and sedatives.

perOption.a: CPAP must be used every night to work.
perOption.b: Consistent use keeps the airway open during all sleep.
perOption.c: Sedatives worsen airway collapse in sleep apnea.
perOption.d: Mask problems should be fixed, not used as a reason to stop.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach CPAP use for sleep apnea.

questions.stem: A client with fractured ribs is taking shallow breaths because of pain. Which intervention is most important to prevent complications?

options.text: Wrap the chest tightly with an elastic bandage
Give adequate pain relief and encourage deep breathing while splinting with a pillow
Keep the client on bed rest
Limit fluids

rationale.correct: Pain control and deep breathing prevent atelectasis and pneumonia after rib fractures.

perOption.a: Binding the chest limits expansion and raises the risk of pneumonia.
perOption.b: Pain control allows deep breathing and coughing, preventing atelectasis and pneumonia.
perOption.c: Immobility increases respiratory complications.
perOption.d: Limiting fluids thickens secretions.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent pulmonary complications after rib fractures.
